utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Wednesday, February 4th, 2009, and I welcome the representatives of the OTP. I welcome Mr. Seselj and everyone helping us. We will soon move into closed session, because we have a witness with protective measures. However, two words first. Mr. Seselj, last time you told us during the hearing that you had some difficulties contacting Mr. Karadzic [Realtime transcript read in error "Krasic"]. The Trial Chamber has just found out about this -- Karadzic, not Krasic, Karadzic. I would like the interpreters to be very careful when I talk, and I would like my words to be conveyed exactly. I don't like to have to see the screen all time and check the screen all the time to make sure that my words are correctly translated. I believe I understood, Mr. Seselj, that last time you were banned from talking to Mr. Karadzic. Well, I can tell you that this Trial Chamber did not intervene at all, and we just discovered this problem. But I believe I've just understood that the measure has been lifted and that now you can talk with this -- with Mr. Karadzic, if you wish to. This is what I wanted to say. Now, this being said, I would like the usher to please drop the blinds because we will bring in the witness, this witness who has protective measures, and I would like the Registrar to move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We can just arrange for the blinds up so the interpreters don't get too much noise in their headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, have you held any positions of a political nature in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From early childhood, I was active, first of all, as an athlete, and I also took part in some cultural activities. After I grew up and matured, (redacted) (redacted) At the age of 17, I was -- I joined the League of Communists of the former Yugoslavia. And a year later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Witness, avoid giving place names, which could identify you. Registrar, please prepare an order so that the name of the village, page 55, line 14, is redacted. It's not your fault, but we shall keep an eye on this. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that, I was elected secretary of the party organisation in the place I lived in, and that lasted for two years. After that, I was the secretary of the local commune, with a mandate of several years. And all that went on up until the outbreak of the war and conflict in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you elected a councillor for a particular party at some point, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. At the beginning of the multiparty system in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was elected president of the Party of Democratic Action in my town, and by virtue of that office, a member of the Municipal Board of the Party of Democratic Action as well. After that, I was elected secretary of the municipal organisation of the Party of the Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Judges how the relationship was between the different ethnic groups in your village before the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the conflict, there were no national tensions in my village. We lived -- we were on friendly terms, good neighbourly terms, without any ethnic divisions. However, with the advent of the multiparty system, there was a certain separation with different views of things, and there was additional pressure by the leaders, if I can put it that way, the leaders of the nationalist parties, and the tensions grew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What parties are you referring to when you talk about nationalist parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I meant the SDS party, that is, the Serbian Democratic Party, and the SDA party, the Party of Democratic Action, and the party that was in the territory which was Mr. Seselj's party, the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these leaders that you refer to, could you give us the name of those, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will state the names of people, of Serbs, but I'm not quite sure whether I could state the names of the people who were strictly the leaders of the SDS or the Serbian Radical Party. Now, in my particular region, where I lived, and there were two villages that were linked together with a purely Muslim population, and one with a mixed population where the Serbs and Muslims lived together, now in that area, in that mixed area, there was (redacted) as being the most prominent. I'm sorry that I haven't got the file now, because I haven't remembered the names of the other people, but if the occasion arises, I'd like to read the names of the other activists who were Serbs. Now, when it comes to the activists in the SDA party, in my area, apart from me, there was some other people --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a question just to shed some light on. There's something that might be unclear because of the translation. Before giving the list of these parties, you called them -- did you call them national parties or nationalistic parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nationalist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I wanted to note, because on the transcript it says "nationalist," whereas the witness has spoken about national parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, in your language, what word do you use for "national"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very easy to clear this up. "National parties" means people belonging to a nation. There were no ethnic Serbs in the Party of Democratic Action, and vice versa, at least not in my town. Later, they became nationalistic. When tensions grew, they became nationalistic, and after that the war broke out. But at this point in time I said that they were, to begin with, national parties, and people joined the different national parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder whether, to be on the safe side, it would be prudent to redact the name at page 57, line 10. I understand we're here talking about a local political leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's redact. Mr. Registrar, line 10, page 57, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, who were -- if you know, who were the political leadership at the top level of these parties, if I can put it that way, at a national level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the Party of Democratic Action, it was Asim Juzbasic who was president of the party at the local level, and the president of the SDS at the municipal level was Branko Grujic. The president of the Serbian Radical Party, I'm not quite sure just now, I'm not sure of his name, because, after all, it's 17 years since that time, and I've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly the answer you have given relate to the municipality of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when -- and I think you've answered that, but just to come back, did there come a time when the situation and relationship between the different ethnic groups in your area changed, and if you could describe how it changed, if it did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As time passed since the formation of the multi-parties or multi-party system in my municipality, tensions grew. There were different opinions of life in general and life together, and so the national leaders used this. They used this opportunity, especially those who had planned to effect certain plans through war, and this led to changes, tension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Zvornik municipality before the conflict, were members of all ethnic groups -- men of all ethnic groups of military age, would they be subject to call-ups in case of mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Before -- or, rather, four days ago [as interpreted], on the 4th of April, 1992, the president of the Serbian Radical Party, Branko Grujic, through the information media, and this was conveyed by the -- by Belgrade Radio, he proclaimed general mobilisation for Serbs living in Zvornik municipality. Now, before -- a long time before that, mobilisation had been carried out in the field, and the Serb population was mobilised. They were armed, units were established, trenches dug, and preparations generally went through for a war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says "Branko Grujic, president of the Serbian Radical Party." I had to intervene, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I might have made a mistake. Branko Grujic was president of the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party. I apologise for that mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, did you have a military booklet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did have a military booklet, just like all the other recruits and conscripts that were over the age of 18, those who had done their military service and who, before the beginning of the war -- or which were taken away, confiscated, before the beginning of the war. And all conscripts were called up, those who had military booklets. They were told to report to the Secretariat of National Defence or the work organisation where they were employed and to bring their military booklets with them and all the military equipment that they had been issued previously. And when it came to my own identity, I can say that I was working in a company, and I had my military booklet and my equipment, and I was registered. And the people sitting there tore out a page from my military booklet where my war assignment was listed, and this was done for all Muslims who were conscripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was it done for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That certainly was not done to the Serbs, and here's why: I worked in a company where the ratio of employees was 50:50 and there was mutual friendship, we socialised, we had family ties, mixed marriages, and so forth, and people would receive information from their true friends, regardless of ethnicity, and I know that that was not done to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any registration made of the men who were called up in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true. Everybody who was called up and whose page was torn out of their military booklet about their ranks and war assignments. Parallel to that, information was recorded about them, their personal information with their place of residence, addresses, telephone numbers and so forth, and I had to do the same. I had to give my address and telephone number so that they had all this evidence and all the information they needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened in February. I'm not 100 percent sure, but at least before the war broke out. That means February 1992. And for some, that happened earlier, depending on the areas and places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the Serb dug trenches. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I said a moment ago that the area I lived in was bordering on an area that was predominantly inhabited by Serbs, there was a road that linked up the two that led to the town of Zvornik, and people would pass by along that road, and they would notice that trenches were being dug and that there were patrols, that people, Serbs, were patrolling the area in groups of twos or threes, sometimes quite informally. But, anyway, they let it be known that they were standing guard, patrolling the area, and so forth. And you could feel this also when the communication -- the buses couldn't pass by that way, or they were stopped going from a Serb area to a Muslim area. Some reason was given, but, anyway, transport was stopped. And the Muslims noted this, so they had to choose a roundabout road if they wished to go that way. Traffic was stopped on the other one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so it's clear, who stopped the traffic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The leadership, the political leadership on the Serb side, regardless of the parties, their political leadership, Serb political leadership. And I said that (redacted) was the main responsible person, the alpha and omega, the be all and end all in that area, of course with permission from Branko Grujic, and his acquiescence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, once again, when was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war operations broke out. And in Zvornik, war broke out on the 8th of April, so this means it was sometime in February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there any meetings held by the Serbian leadership in your area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meetings were held in all the areas of Zvornik municipality, in all parts, and also in the place where I lived. So meetings were held all over, and we received information -- or, rather, I personally learnt this from my friends and acquaintances who were Serbs and who were my friends and from others, too, who had friends among the Serbs, among the Serb population. And as I said at the beginning, where I lived, there were a lot of mixed marriages and friendships between the two ethnicities, so they -- the Muslims would always have information from their friends, and they told them that the situation in the area was very bad and their friends, the Serbs, warned them that there would be an escalation, and war operations might break out, and that they should leave the area or at least get their children -- women and children and elderly away from the area. So we were warned by them. We did receive that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Jovo Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted), in actual fact, and I do know him, yes. I came to work one morning, and Jovo, on the table in front of him, had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, we need to redact this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this name will come up. I think if we redact maybe that the witness shared an office with this person, we would have taken care of the matter. Many people knew this particular person. We'll come back to who he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, let's redact. Just tell him the person that you were sharing your office with, and that way the witness will know who you're talking about. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, you were explaining something about some maps. What is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Now, do you want me to mention the name of this man or not to mention it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What we should avoid is that you -- you explain the details of how you know him. We're protecting your identity, but I think this person is very well known and he knows so, many people that it's not a problem that you mention the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see. Very well, yes. The person in question is someone I know, and I know him because he drew maps of a Greater Serbia. And when I had contacts with him, since we were friends, I asked him why he was doing that, and I warned him that that was not a good idea, and that it didn't lead anywhere and that the media would publish those maps. And we joked about it and had a slight disagreement, but jokingly, about some of the details, because some of the lines on that map went over into another area belonging to another ethnic group. And his answer was -- he said to me that there would be compensation on the other side and that everybody would be satisfied and well served. Now, several days later at the next meeting, this map, the map drawn by this person, did indeed appear in all the newspapers, both in Serbia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he said that there would be compensation, did he say anything about what would happen to the people -- say the Muslims who were living in the Serb areas, for example, what would happen to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- well, he said that if the Muslims did not wish to live in a republic like that, with those borders and with a predominantly Serb population, then exchanges would take place, exchanges of property, houses, and that the people would move out. That was his idea, and it's particularly interesting to note that he was a key politician in Zvornik municipality. He was even a national deputy in the Assembly at the time in the BH Parliament, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I didn't want to cut you off, but I have a question for you. This person who we do not mention who was drawing the map, and the map was published, then he would explain that some arrangement could be found amongst the population. But when he was saying this, was he saying this on his own volition, or was he just repeating what others had said previously, or was it really something that came from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a good question. Thank you for asking that. I can only assume, although I wasn't in his head to know exactly, that these were ideas from a joint global place or decision, leaders, political leaders, and things -- people like that in the Zvornik municipality, since he was a key personage for politics in Zvornik on the side of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you receive these maps and have this discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, once again, but it was at the beginning of March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving to another topic: Did you ever attend any meetings where the accused participated as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And if I can be frank, I'm very pleased that I see the accused, Vojislav Seselj, seven years on minus one month, to see him again, because I had the opportunity of seeing him at a meeting or promotion of the Serbian Radical Party, this time in Mali Zvornik, a small town opposite Veliki Zvornik or Bosanski Zvornik, as it's called.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 17 years on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to say that I admired Vojislav Seselj. It was a long time ago, and he might remember the date of this. And when he became the youngest PhD holder in Yugoslavia, our blood boiled -- or, rather, we thought how wonderful it was to have such a young man, the youngest man with a PhD in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It sort of was somebody with a university training, who'd been to university, and saw that people should be respected and that people should be loved, should love one another, and who learnt that you cannot destroy a people through war. So I was very interested, it was sort of inspiring, and I wondered how it came into Dr. Seselj's head to change overnight and to think that he could destroy a whole nation in a criminal way, with genocide and so on. It was two weeks before the aggression against Zvornik. That means it might have been on the 17th or 18th of March, roughly, 1992, in Mali Zvornik. I saw posters in public places all over Bosanski Zvornik, informing us of the arrival as Vojislav Seselj, the president of the Serbian Radical Party, saying that he was coming to Mali Zvornik. Now, why he decided to do this in Mali Zvornik, in Serbia, probably because Bosanski Zvornik had a kind of structure -- or, rather, the ratio was 64 to 36 in favour of the Muslim population. That was the percentage. I went with a few of my acquaintances to Mali Zvornik, to the place where the rally was being held. It was by the hydroelectric power-plant, downstream, half a kilometre downstream, and I saw a large group of people, I would say maybe even a thousand people, standing in front of the cultural centre, youth cultural centre, and I learnt from people 'round about that the rally would be held outside in the open air. And I assume Mr. Seselj thought or his associates thought that it wouldn't be a good idea to hold the rally there because there were more Muslims than Serbs there, so they decided to hold the rally in the cultural centre itself. And with a few of my friends and acquaintances, I went straight to the cultural centre. I was curious to see the man, who that man was, the man that I had heard such wonderful things about. What did he have to say? How was he going to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you for one minute, and just so we get some of these things -- important details out. Now, you said that there were, in your estimate, around a thousand people outside the cultural dom, and I understand that there was some Muslims and some Serbs. What was the relationship, in your estimate, between the size of the two groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was hard to estimate because I didn't know all the people, but I know a lot of people from Zvornik, from Mali Zvornik. I lived there, went out there. It was difficult to tell what the ratio was in that large group of people. But it was the assessment of Mr. Seselj, his associates, or the organisers of the meeting, that it would not be warm enough to have the meeting outside, because in that part of Mali Zvornik there are two large neighbourhoods populated mostly by Muslims, and a large number of Muslims came out of curiosity from Veliki Zvornik, and also as a protest, expressing their disagreement with this manner of calling people to nationalism, to war, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so I understand that you went inside the cultural centre or the cultural dom. Could you describe how the room looked when you came in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered the room, it was in the basement, the room was dark. There were candles burning, and it was, let me put it that way, traditional orange lights. Let me explain that. I watched a lot of films from World War II where the Chetniks, precisely in this way, had their meetings in darkened rooms, with candles, and with their traditional insignia. You could see the same thing in the cultural hall in Mali Zvornik, the Chetnik flags at prominent places, the table where Mr. Seselj and his associates were supposed to sit. There were hats with the traditional cockades, indicating Chetnik-hood. They entered -- as I entered the hall, and looking around, I could see that in the last row of the hall next to me, there were about 15 to 20 people whom I personally knew. They were Muslims. In the front row, right in front of the table, where Mr. Seselj was supposed to sit, I saw a lot of familiar faces, including Branko Grujic. I said at the beginning that he was president of the Serbian Radical Party -- I apologise again, the Serbian Democratic Party in Zvornik. And at the meeting, he was there, where Mr. Seselj was the president of the Serbian Radical Party. There were a lot of other people who I saw there whom I knew, and I was very surprised at what they were doing there. I was wondering how come that all these people whom I knew, who were in the reserve forces of the JNA and with whom I worked, were suddenly in the front row of this meeting. Suddenly, Mr. Seselj came in with his bodyguards, and from the door he literally said, "God help you, brother Chetniks," and everybody traditionally replied the return greeting, "God help you, hero." They said that altogether. I can still hear Mr. Seselj saying that. He took his place where he was meant to sit, and then after briefly consulting with his associates, he stood up and he began to speak. He said that he was sorry that the meeting -- the rally could not be held outside, for objective reasons, probably meaning for security reasons, and that he hoped that people who were present inside would literally convey to their home organisations what his message was. He underscored again, "I hope that you are true representatives of the groups that were formed in your home units, entities." I can still hear his words in my years that I will never forget, "Brothers, Chetniks, Chetnik brothers," he literally says -- had said, "The time has come for us to give the balijas tit for tat." I will explain. "Balijas" is a derogatory word for Muslims. You've probably had the opportunity to hear this word before in prior testimonies. "The Drina, the River Drina, is not a boundary between Serbia and Bosnia. It is the backbone of the Serbian state. Every foot of land inhabited by Serbs is Serbian land. Let's rise up, Chetnik brothers, especially you from across the Drina. You are the bravest." These are literally his words. I will never forget them, "let us show the balijas, the Turks and the Muslims," he said all of those words in one context, "the green transversal, the direction to the east. That's where their place is." I couldn't stand it anymore. I personally stood up, and I addressed him, "Mr. Seselj --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before we go into that, just so the record is clear, you said that -- it says in the transcript: "The Drina -- the Drina River is not the boundary between Serbia and Bosnia, it is the backbone of the Serbian state." Is that what you remember Mr. Seselj, the accused, saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember this 100 percent. I can never forget those words. That's why I stood up and reacted the way that I reacted. And I would like to state what my reaction was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was not in quotation marks in the transcript, so it was not entirely clear who that was attributed to, but that's clear now. And so you stood up. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, "Mr. Seselj, you can't do this." I knew I wouldn't have enough time to say what I thought and what I wanted to, that I would be interrupted, so that is why I spoke quickly, and I said the following: "Mr. Seselj, this can't be done like this. I came here out of curiosity to see Seselj, the youngest doctor of law and the person who completed the Faculty of Law in Sarajevo in Bosnia-Herzegovina," the person who throughout his life had learned all those things I mentioned at the beginning, and that is that no nation can destroy another nation, "You are inciting people to war. It cannot be like this, Mr. Seselj. This can't be, so I was hoping that you would make a meeting. I, as a member of the youth movement, a Tito's pioneer --" everyone knows that Tito was the president of Yugoslavia, where we all lived as brothers, and nobody paid any attention to the ethnic origin of anyone else, so I said, "I, as Tito's youth member, expected you to give a different speech against war, against nationalism," and I did manage to complete what I was saying after -- everybody got disturbed. Two of his bodyguards took me under -- by the arms, and without violence or anything. They just carried me outside, threw me out. When I was out, I could hear objections, whistling by a large group of people who were asking that the meeting be held outside, that Seselj should go out and explain this to the people outside. There was a large number of policemen from Serbia, of course, because according to the regulations the Bosnian police could not be on the territory of another republic. Five or six minutes after that, Seselj, with his associates, left the hall, and then there was a general fight that broke out. I was in the parking-lot just there next to a group of people, and I happened to know some of these people, and one of the people opened the back of his trunk of his car, and he said, "Chetnik brothers, take this." And I could see that the trunk was piled full of pieces of wood, of timber about an inch or two thick. They were like wooden poles about 70 or 80 metres long. And the group of young people who were there took those pieces of wood, those planks, and then a general fight broke out. You really couldn't tell who was hitting who. You couldn't tell who was a Serb, who was a Muslim. Objects began flying through the air, and at one point I could see a large -- very large group of people who were lying on the ground. I assume that they probably knocked him down -- that Seselj's bodyguards knocked him down to protect him from the blows. The next day, I saw in a newspaper Mr. Seselj with a band-aid on his face and with a bandaged hand. He's not close to me right now, but I really wanted to ask him where he got this scar that he has. I wanted to ask him before I began telling about all of this. But, anyway, after a while the people went off, and the area was cleared, and that's how the whole thing ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, I'd like to move on to another topic, and it's -- the general area - and this is what I'd like to focus on - is the Municipal Assembly of Zvornik. And, just very quickly, I'd like to ask you about some of -- some people and whether you can tell us who they are and what position they held. Just in this context, you've already said it, but maybe Branko Grujic, who is he, and what position did he have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Branko Grujic was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party. He was a key figure or, rather, a person who everyone else had to listen to, listen to the proposals he made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position, if any, did he have in the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't have any particular position in the Municipal Assembly, because he was involved in private business, but probably the scenario was prepared in advance of what would shortly turn out to be that he would become the president of the War Presidency of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Jovo Mijatovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovo Mijatovic, I already spoke about him, was a deputy representing the Serbian people in the Republican Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Jovo Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jovo Ivanovic was the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stevo Radic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stevo Radic was the secretary of the Municipality of Zvornik. As you can see, I am mentioning names of people -- names of Serbs. All the key political posts, regardless of the fact that -- the fact that the ethnic structure in Zvornik was 64 percent to 36 percent in favour of the Muslims, all the key political posts were held by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Please, Witness, there's something I don't understand. You've just said that 64 percent of this municipality was Muslims, 30 percent were Serb, but these people had been elected, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 36 percent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the Muslims that accounted for 64 percent of the population, these people voted, didn't they? How is it, then, that those elected officials were Serbs who were holding the key positions? There's something I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what you are asking, and I'm going to try to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All my questions are excellent questions. Please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's true that they were all deputies and that everyone voted, and that after the first multiparty voting in the Zvornik municipality, this was the ratio, 64 to 36 percent. In fact, the ratio was a little bit narrower, because there was a number of people who did not -- who were actually in the SDP, the League of Communists, so they did not declare themselves as Muslims, but they picked an option that was more universal, that was in between the two. So when the key places in the municipality were being staffed, there was a sense that war was clear, it had already -- war was nearing. It had already began in the Republic of Croatia. Muslims knew what would happen to them in that area, and this is why they made certain concessions in order to keep the peace. They made concessions to the Serbs so that the Serbs occupied more of the key political posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now we understand better, thanks to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it's possible for you to describe, very briefly: In the spring of 1992, what did the Serbs in Zvornik -- what was their political aim, what was their political vision for Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, the political vision or the goal of the Serbs in Zvornik, which they tried to implement through the Parliament also, in the Assembly, was the division of Zvornik into a Serb and Muslim municipality; also the division of the Karakaj Industrial Zone, which was one of the most powerful in Bosnia and Herzegovina, into a Muslim and a Serb part. It was not possible to do this, in view of the percentages that I referred to earlier, especially if you take into account that these two ethnic groups were intermingled, and there was no populated place in that area that had a clear majority among the Serbs or the Muslims. Still, it was the Serbs' option or goal to go for total division, and this is why many meetings took place later, agreements, and we were unable to get anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, what was the counter-position to this wish to divide the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We tried to set up rallies, mass rallies, in the town of Zvornik, and I provided a tape that I had from one of those meetings where you can clearly see that the rally was attended by tens of thousands of people, and these people were addressed by the most prominent figures of the Zvornik municipality, both Serbs and Muslims. Both Muslims and Serbs spoke, those who were against the war, those who were aware that this was not leading anywhere and that it was not a way to reach any solution, it was only the way for one or the other ethnic group to suffer. They were against the war.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Gentlemen, Judges, I believe that the Prosecution would need to make a transcript of this footage tonight and that tomorrow this should be distributed before the start of the cross-examination. If the witness provided this to the Prosecution in time, there is no excuse for this not being done already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit is not on the Prosecution's exhibit list, and we do not intend to tender this particular video into evidence. If the accused wants to tender it into evidence, he's, of course, free to seek its admission, and we would not oppose that. The witness will give evidence about the particular rallies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When did you get this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The Prosecution got this in 1996, when the witness gave his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Seselj has had a copy of this, has he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have the video. You can look at it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what am I supposed to do with it, Mr. President? Where am I going to look at it? The fact that the Prosecutor a few days ago sent some DVD to me, that means nothing to me. There is nobody to look at that for me or to make a transcript for me, and I have no communication with anyone regarding these exhibits. This footage, if the Prosecution did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I will tell you what I think of this. From my own personal experience, we have received the DVDs and videos sent by the Prosecution, and I came here at 5.00 in the morning to watch these videos on my computer, and I watched all of them. Do like me; just get up early, put your videos or your DVDs into your DVD reader, and just watch the videos.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, but on several occasions, as Pre-Trial Judge, you expressly instructed the Prosecution to furnish all documents under 68(1) to me in hard copy, exclusively in hard copy. This video footage is of footage of a rally which the Muslim parties or their leading party organised in Zvornik the day before the armed conflict. If this footage is not a favourable piece of evidence for the Prosecution, it must be a document under Rule 68.1. I am convinced of that. They didn't do that. I don't have a computer in my cell, I don't know how to use one, and I'm not in the position to look at any DVDs or materials on my video player.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you feel that this video is important, I don't know, during your cross-examination you can ask to see it. That will not be a problem. Witness, this video, I'm sure I've seen it, but I've seen so many that I couldn't tell you what's on this video. I assume that the video shows a crowd of people. That's what it's about, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. But it's not true, what Mr. Seselj said, that it was held on the day before the aggression on Zvornik. This footage is of a rally that was held several days before. There is another meeting that I can talk about was held on the day before the actual aggression, and I can talk about that after I see the video. I can talk about that later, if I am asked to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On what date was this video shot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that before the aggression in Zvornik, it was three or four days before that, so it could have been either on the 4th or 5th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the statement of this witness, it says that this was on the 6th and 7th of April. This is on page 5 of the statement. So I'm now reframing from any kind of comments, but I really must say this: These are two rallies on the eve of the outbreak of the conflict, and the witness himself said "6th and 7th of April." You can see that on page 3, paragraph 2. But if you believe that the Prosecution was not obliged to disclose that to me in an appropriate manner, what can I do? I have to submit to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there were two rallies, seemingly, one on the 4th and 5th and the other one on the 6th or 7th. The video refers to the first rally or the second one? It's difficult, I know, 17 years later, to answer that question. I understand fully. If you don't know, say so, just say you can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I state with 100 percent certainty, and I did state a solemn declaration that I would be speaking the truth, so this is the footage of the first rally, before the second one that was held a day before the conflict. If I said that it was on the 5th or 6th, I mean this was 17 years ago, so I don't know. If this is so important to Mr. Seselj whether it was on the 5th or the 6th, I mean, it's 24-hours difference. The point is that it was the first rally and not the second rally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you really insist that the Prosecution does not have to submit this document to me, I'm not going to make any more objections. But I would like to remind you that after this rally, all the Serbs left Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. Seselj, the Prosecutor has given you this video. You have it. You've had it for a long time. That's all there is to it. The Prosecutor doesn't want to show it. He does what he likes. If you wish to show it, you can bring it along or you can say to the Registrar tomorrow that you wish to display it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could have asked your associates to show it and ask them whether it's in any way important for your Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely what I mentioned when you discussed this. I said to you, since you have all these DVDs, just give these to Mr. Krasic or somebody else, ask these people to look at all this footage, get up early in the morning, and then they can get back to you and tell you whether there's anything interesting in these videos. I understand that you don't have time to watch these images, since you have tens of thousands of documents to read, so I don't hold this against you, but I did say that you could ask your associates to watch these images, and I remember telling you this. Whatever the case may be, this video shows a gathering. I don't think this is a very determining factor. Maybe it is. It will be for you to say so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I know, the Prosecution gave me that footage a few days ago. I don't know the exact date. But this is not the same footage that was provided to me a few years ago. And, finally, as of October 1st, I have no associates, practically no associates. Since we have a protected witness again, I cannot speak about him or his testimony with Mr. Krasic. You have forbidden me to do that in a written decision, which you have decided to make public yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but when I told you to give the DVD to your associates, this was several months ago. I said this several months ago already, and at the time there wasn't a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the Prosecutor just tell us what date it was that he gave me this DVD?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, do you have the acknowledgment of receipt when you disclosed this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't, but I did wish to state that in fairness to the accused, we had not been able to determine an early disclosure, so we disclosed the -- we disclosed the video sometime, I think, late last week. So the accused is correct, he has not had the DVD that we're currently talking about for a very long time. Obviously, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, you said the opposite a while ago. You said that this video had been disclosed. I can't remember in what year. A long time ago. So you disclosed this video last week; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: On the 2nd of February, Your Honours. And the -- of course, the video itself is mentioned in the witness statement of -- from 2002, I believe, if it's not even in the statement from 1996, so if this particular video was so important to the accused, it's certainly something that could have been raised earlier than today. I have not -- I don't understand what's said on the video, but I've had it reviewed for the purpose of this case, and I can inform Your Honours of the contents of it. It is, as Your Honour has pointed out, a recording of a rally. From what I understand, it's very difficult in many parts to hear what is being said, but the general theme is -- expressed by the speakers is that there should be no ethnic division. The speakers are opposed to this. They want a multiethnic Zvornik. There's absolutely nothing exculpatory in that material, and as I said, we're not tendering this exhibit into evidence. We have disclosed it to the accused so that he have it, because we thought that he should have the material that was provided by this witness and is described in his statement, but there's absolutely nothing exculpatory in it, as far as I can see from the description that I've been given of this video. I think we might be wasting our time here, and we should maybe simply get on with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so. Mr. Seselj, you were disclosed this video on the 2nd of February. This is what Mr. Marcussen has just said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank Mr. Marcussen for that very correct way in which he has behaved. I haven't been accustomed to that by a representative of the OTP. I thought it was given to me last week, at the end of last week. He said the 2nd, which is Monday, which is the day before yesterday. What are we today, the 7th? What -- what's the date? Anyway, it was the day before yesterday that I received it, and that's the rally after which all the Serbs fled Zvornik, and it's the rally that was held on the day Bosnia and Herzegovina's independence was proclaimed. And you know the terrible bitterness that the Serbs felt when they heard about Bosnia's independence being recognised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, do you remember the Assembly met on the 3rd of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember the meeting held on the 3rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A meeting was held. All citizens of goodwill were invited to attend and to profess their views and opposition to all national divisions, the divisions of towns, the infrastructure, to speak up against war, and for a time this had positive echoes. After that, there were a series of political meetings held by the leadership, both Muslim and Serb. And after all that, there was a meeting with the army, the Yugoslav People's Army, led by a man called Jankovic. And, quite literally, assistance was asked. The Yugoslav Army was asked to assist or to give guarantees that Zvornik would be peaceful and that there wouldn't be a war, and that nothing would happen there that had happened in the neighbouring town, where killings had already taken place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you want to make a break, I have one more objection. Now, suddenly, the Prosecutor has introduced an Assembly, a meeting that I have never heard of, of the 3rd of April. I know about the 6th and 7th of April meetings and rallies. That makes it two, plus this 3rd of April meeting, or is the Prosecutor referring to the meetings of the 6th and 7th of April? This is something that is completely unknown in all the material we've seen so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I thought I understand that a meeting had been held the day that Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed independence. We know that. Apparently it seems that there was another one either before or after. We're sort of lost. Which one are you referring to, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not referring to any meetings, the witness is. And I will try to clarify some of these things. But there's nothing for the accused to object to. He's on full notice of the evidence of this witness, and actually, he has been provided a chronology that the witness has drafted up himself. So there's no basis for the objection. If Your Honours want to take a break, we can do it now, and I will get back and clarify all these dates and meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, try and shed some light on this during the break so that we will know later on how many rallies were held, you know, so the witness will tell us exactly when these meetings were held, because obviously there were rallies held by Mr. Seselj, and then there were other meetings that were organised on the Muslim side, and it's not very clear. So please try to shed some light on this over the break. I believe you have about an hour left. You've used up an hour already. The best would be if you could finish your examination-in-chief today. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, we talked about a meeting that was held on the 3rd of April. Where was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to say I'm sorry that there was a misunderstanding earlier on over the number of meetings and their dates. We were talking about two mass rallies, antiwar rallies of citizens, and we set the date there. One was held on the 5th or 6th, and the last on the 7th. Now, the meeting that we're talking about now, the 3rd of April meeting, that was a meeting between the political parties of the Muslims and Serbs, and it was held in the Municipal Assembly building and headquarters in Zvornik, where they tried to reach an agreement about the possibilities of avoiding war or, rather, to find a way out of the situation by meeting the military leaders and ask the armies guarantees for a peaceful life and a life together in the municipality of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a proposal made from the Muslim side as to what could be done to ensure peace, any concrete measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that the Muslim side put forward a proposal, the one I talked about a moment ago; that is to say, that the army should guarantee peace and that all the barricades should be abolished that the Serbs had set up along the outskirts of the town or towards the industrial zone towards Tuzla and Karakaj and other built-up areas. And if there was no possibility of continuing a normal life together in communality, and if the municipality needed to be divided, the infrastructure of the municipality, that that could go ahead just to avoid a war. That was the main thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On -- if you remember, on what date was the meeting with Jankovic held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting with General Jankovic, the commander of the Tuzla Corps, was held on the 7th, in the afternoon or at around noon, in the premises of the Municipal Assembly building of Zvornik, where a document was supposed to be signed officially about life together, and togetherness and communality, and doing away with the barricades, just like the meeting that had started on the 3rd and was postponed until the 5th. And Jovo Ivanovic came to one of those meetings, the president of the Municipal Assembly, who said, quite literally, that he had come to the meeting but that the Serb side wished no -- to have no negotiations but an -- exclusively a division. He came to say that he did not want negotiations, but a division. But on pressure from General Jankovic, it was nonetheless agreed that coexistence must be maintained, and all tension must be surpassed. And on the 7th, that's when that second meeting or rally took place, the one that Mr. Seselj mentioned, in the afternoon, that is to say, after 12.00 noon. And a large number of people, thousands of people, came to in front of the municipal building. There were loud-speakers and microphones, and the people went on discussing and sayings things that they said at the first rally against the war and against things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to go back to the 6th of April. Was there a Municipal Assembly meeting on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, a Municipal Assembly meeting was held on that precise day. I attended. However, let me repeat again. The firm resolve of the political leadership and deputies on the Serb side was that there should be no negotiations and no solutions about continuing coexistence in town. And this could be felt, of course, because the citizens -- the Serb citizens had already left the town, and they'd gone towards Serbia, across the Drina River or elsewhere, so it was at that meeting that the conclusion was made; that is to say, on the 6th, they decided to hold another urgent meeting with the army and the army should provide guarantees. And after that meeting, the key figures should address the public on radio -- over Radio Zvornik, key figures on both sides, and one member of the army, that they should speak over the radio and tell the citizens to remove the barricades and to quell tension so that coexistence could continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you -- do you remember whether Branko Grujic made any particular statements at that meeting at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. He said especially that there should be no negotiations, no further discussions. He said, "We are setting apart the police, the Serb police. We're going to separate the Serb police," and that's what he did. And the Serb policemen separated themselves into the industrial zone of Karakaj or, more exactly, the textile factory that was called Alhos. That was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it at some point become clear to you that the situation would develop into an armed struggle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at some point think that there would be an armed struggle in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was quite clear to me, personally, as it was to everybody else, that war was imminent, especially because of the presence of a large number of soldiers and organised units stationed in the neighbouring republic, in Serbia, and others, Radalj, Loznica, Koviljaca, and along the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this information -- I was given this information from a friend and from my acquaintances, and they lived in Loznica, Koviljaca, and those border areas in Serbia, so when they came to work, they would talk about this and say that war was imminent; that there was a large number of soldiers, regular and irregular troops, which means that there were those who were not exclusively the JNA but volunteers; and that a large number of technical equipment and materiel had been stationed along the border and was directed towards Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it possible for you to tell us at what time you received this information? When are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was before. The information about the stationing and positioning of the army in the localities I've just mentioned is information that I received perhaps eight or nine or ten days before from people who had either seen the units or heard about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would I be correctly summing up what you have said is that the Serb position was that there should be a division of Zvornik, and if that could not be agreed upon, then there would be a conflict, and it would be settled -- this issue would be settled with arms; is that a correct summary of how you understood the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a correct summary of all the negotiations, meetings, rallies. All of them led to the conclusion that there was absolutely no chance for negotiation anymore. There was one more chance, in actual fact, for negotiation, when the head of the municipality, Abdulah Pasic, at the invitation of someone, probably the army, had to go to a meeting in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. We will get to that in just one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have an additional detail from the witness. You said that the information on the imminent threat of war was something that you received eight, nine days before, but before what? I didn't understand before what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the aggression itself on the 8th of April. That's when the aggression started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your recollection today, were there ever anyone who explicitly said that if the Muslim side did not accept a division, then there would be a war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that sentence came from Brano Grujic. He said, "If you gentlemen Muslims don't want us to divide up the town and the industrial zone so that we can be completely separate, then there will be war."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he say that? Sorry, when did he say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that at the last meeting on the 6th, the last meeting held on the 6th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What day did the -- did the majority of the Serbs leave Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs started leaving Zvornik slowly, and this was noticeable, about seven or eight days before, and then they intensified their departure three to four days before the aggression was unleashed, because according to some plan and project, they were supposed to -- the aggression on Zvornik was supposed to start on the 4th of April, but with the negotiations that took place, that dead-line was prolonged for the beginning of the war against Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, does this mean that the Serbs knew that the aggression was going to happen a few days later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim quite definitely that the Serbs knew there would be an aggression, because their political leaders had conducted preparations much before, preparing the units, creating crisis staffs, patrolling the area; unnecessary, in my opinion. These Serbs patrolled the areas along the border belt and where the Serbs were the majority. And the very fact that the Serbs moved out of the Zvornik area and the town of Zvornik itself meant that there was war in the air. You could smell it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could smell it, and the Muslims could smell it or feel it. That's one thing. But how is it that this information on an imminent threat of war would be only confined to the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that information was accessible to everyone, to all the ethnicities and population of Zvornik. But since the Muslims did not want -- well, there were Serbs who didn't want it, either, but the Muslims didn't especially, and that's why I said that at the rally that was held, the Serbs demonstrated that they were against the war and for coexistence, but the Muslims hoped that people wouldn't leave their homes. It's difficult to leave your homes and send your family away or go into a war unprepared. Why? Because the Muslims didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, you talked about a last chance for peace and a meeting attended by Pasic. You should know that we have heard other evidence about that particular meeting, but if very briefly you could just tell us, when did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting took place after the rally of the 7th of April, in front of the Municipal Assembly building. The army, led by Jankovic, turned up, or rather they received orders from somewhere or instructions that in Mali Zvornik a meeting should be held of politicians, Muslim politicians and Serb politicians, together with the army. I was never quite clear on why. I never discussed this with anyone. But later on I learnt that this meeting took place at the Jezero Hotel, which is half a kilometre downstream from the hydroelectric power-plant on the Drina River, and that meeting was attended personally by Arkan himself. Later on, I learnt that Arkan threatened the Serbs and said that if they put their signature to an agreement for coexistence and peace, there would -- that he personally, with his soldiers, would intervene, step in and kill the Serbs. I heard this from others. I didn't hear it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I guess it would be a fair assessment that the meeting was unsuccessful. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that meeting was unsuccessful. The Muslim politicians returned home, and later on I learnt, and they were ashamed to say this, that they had even been physically mistreated; that is to say that Arkan slapped them because they wanted to confirm what had been agreed with the army earlier on in the municipality building on the 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the Muslim side, once the delegation came back from the Jezero Hotel, were there an effort made to organise some sort of crisis committee or something like that on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that we waited for the Muslim politicians to return from the meeting from Mali Zvornik, where we were quite literally told that there were no more chances for negotiation and that Zvornik would be attacked, and that there was no other way out but to set up a crisis staff which would attempt to organise and pull out the population, the civilians, women, children, and use the roads that were still passable in the direction of Tuzla. And in the first wave, there was a mass exodus towards (redacted), and the Snagovo area, and also the area of Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a brief second. We would, I think, Your Honour, ask if we could redact page 92, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, were efforts made also to organise some sort of defence of Zvornik at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since the Muslim people didn't have weapons because the Serb police seized all the weapons that were placed in the police garages and moved it to Karakaj, to the newly-formed police administration or station there, so the Muslims did not have a chance to organise themselves in the town itself, maybe some people did have their own personal weapons. I don't know about that. Perhaps hunting weapons, since there were many hunters in that area. It was something that was very popular in the Zvornik area. In some re-border areas, perhaps there were some guards to stop incursions from Serbs at least until the civilians pulled out. Later, when the Crisis Staff was trying to get out, and I was a member of it, when we were trying to get out to Kula Grad -- it's a settled area at an elevation from where you could see the entire town of Zvornik below.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, in the interests of time I'm going to jump somewhat in time, I think, and I'd like to ask you: Are you familiar with a place sometimes referred to as Djuza's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Djuza's house, yes. It's the house of a woman whose name is Djuza, Djuza Salihovic. It's a well-known house because there was a prisoner camp in that house, and it was opened on the 25th or the 26th of May. The Serbs -- well, I'll go in order. On the 23rd and 24th of May, Serbs, or the army -- it wasn't the regular army, it was the paramilitary force, came to the area of Liplje, to the school there, and was seizing the weapons. The Muslims hurriedly handed over the weapons that they had, hunting weapons perhaps, whatever else they had managed to obtain through other channels. They handed over the weapons and they called for life together. If they handed over their weapons, they were told that they would get some passes to be able to go to town to get some food and things like that. Anyway, when this was done, on the 25th or 26th, I think that's when it started, the assembling of all the population, assembling them all together in a very big house, a three-floor house, Djuza's house, and the people were placed there and in surrounding areas, and there were 483 prisoners located in that camp. Very soon after that, they were tortured, beaten, raped, asked to provide specific information. Their money and valuables, gold, jewellery, were taken from them. All of this was taking place not far from where I was, where I had a very good view of the Serbs' movements as they were bringing in the prisoners. It occurred to me that we had to organise ourselves and to free those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. How far were you from Djuza's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my vantage point, it was perhaps a kilometre as the crow flies, or maybe even less. I cannot really tell you exactly. But you could plainly see, and especially if you had binoculars, then you could clearly see people, their faces. So some women -- some people -- some women that I saw, I could actually tell who they were if I looked through the binoculars. They had to walk around without their clothing, in front of a group of soldiers who were sitting on some crates from which they were drinking alcohol, actually beer. That's what I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever having conversations with anyone who had been at Djuza's house about what happened? And don't mention any names, but did you ever speak to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four days after the camp was formed at Djuza's house, one girl, a little girl, escaped from the camp. She managed to escape a rape, and I'll explain how it happened. Since she knew me and since she found out from someone or was asking who would be able to help her, then I spoke with her privately, and she said that she had escaped from being raped by using a kind of trick, saying she wasn't ready. She was bruised and her clothing was torn, and she explained to me where this took place, which house she was, and in which houses around Djuza's house women and girls were taken to be raped and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were efforts made to -- no, sorry. No, we can go on with this. Were efforts made -- efforts made to free the people who were detained at Djuza's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two attempts, one right after this young girl fled the camp. (redacted), if people had any weapons left, to find some people who still hadn't handed over their weapons, to try to free those people. And it's true that there were many of those who wanted to go into this action to liberate the camp, who had their relatives, close relatives, and I don't mention their names, in the camp. But this never actually materialised because there were no weapons and people were not -- there wasn't enough courage to go with their bare hands up against 60 armed Serbian soldiers, which is the information I had, 60 Chetniks in that area, and they were divided into two areas. One was in school and the other one perhaps some 200 or 250 metres further in Djuza's house and the neighbouring houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, because of the nature of the information, the specificity of the information, I think we would have to redact page 94, line 22: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. To be on the safe side, it would be better. So, Registrar, could you please redact line 22 and after on page 94. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, was there -- did you participate later on in an attack to free the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, I did take part in such an organised action on the 2nd of June, 1992, when the camp was actually liberated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please explain to the Judges what you saw when you came to the camp? What was the situation of the detainees? What did you see as you went to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not going to talk about the actual method and how we approached the camp because of the time available, but as we were approaching the camp and were trying to liberate it house by house, while we were approaching the camp, just 15 metres away from me a woman came out of a cellar, leading a boy by the hand. From that same house some six metres away, she was shot at and hit with two bullets. This all took place very close to me, some five or six metres away, because I was behind a house that was nearby. The most horrible scene was when her son, who was five years old, tried to pick her up. He tried to lift her, and his hand was -- his hands were bloody. And he was calling his mother to stand up, to get up, but it was too late. I could see blood flowing from the wounds, the two wounds in her body. I tried to save the child, and in the second attempt my friend managed to grab the child and save him. And as we were closer to the camp, some ten metres away, some -- sheltering behind some sort of low wall, a Serbian soldier was ordering, "Pick up all your things, destroy what you cannot carry, and let's escape in this direction." I was looking at him, but I couldn't do anything because there was firing coming from all sides, also in the direction where I was with my friends. When he opened the door -- he kicked the door open. I could hear his voice, "Take the scarves, the shawls -- the sheets so that this can be seen, some scum is killing us." These are the words that I heard this man say. Anyway, later I found out that the nickname of that man is Brzi. I cannot remember his first and last name, but I have it written down somewhere. He's a man who was working in a construction company as a crane operator in Belgrade, and he was from the area nearby where this event was taking place. The prisoners started running out, and I managed to raise my hand. And because some were already beginning to run after this soldier, and they didn't know what was happening, I shouted at them to start moving towards me. And then he moved away from a post and fired a burst of fire at all of those people. After the people left the house, there were many of those who had gone in different directions. Eight persons were left at that place, and they had been actually killed and died on the spot. I don't know their names, but later I was there -- in there when they were being buried. It was horrible to see a 12-year-old girl whose brains had fallen out of her head, and later I had to put them back. Anyway, I could see the direction in which this man who fired at all of those people escaped, but I couldn't get to him, so I couldn't reach him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- you mentioned that you had been told that women were being raped. Once you were in the camp, did you see anything which led you to -- did you see any more evidence that this had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's true that after the action, when the houses were being searched, I found a woman that I actually knew. Her head -- actually, her neck had been twisted. She had been strangled. She was sitting on a couch, and the lower -- the clothing on the lower part of her body was removed. She was sitting on this couch. Later, her body was taken by her family, and we buried her together with those others who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that we go into private session for some additional information, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VS-2000, the President has asked that we try to finish your evidence today, and just so you know, we have 15 minutes left. There's one more topic that I'd like to try to cover in those 15 minutes. After the events we have talked about, did you receive information about the detention of Muslims at Karakaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, I did have information about Muslims detained in Karakaj. In my area where I lived, there were many refugees from the town itself, because that is that area that I was talking about at the beginning where people had left certain areas and were trying to get to the largest stretch of free territory towards Tuzla. So when the camp was freed, there were three bodies there of soldiers, Serbs who had been keeping or guarding the camp, three bodies. Then I was called personally from a check-point, a line of separation between the Serb and Muslim forces. They called me and said that there was a man from Belgrade who wanted to speak to me. I went up, covering a distance of about 100 or 150 metres as the crow flies, and I tried to speak with him. He asked me to explain what the man looked like who was found in that area. He was looking for a certain man, trying to see if he had been killed. I described the man, the Serb soldiers that I saw, and he took his head with both of his hands and said that that was his brother. And he was showing me this truck, and he showed me that he was offering a whole truck of flour, sugar, oil, a lot of food, to have his brother's body returned. I said we didn't need any of those food items, even though we didn't have them; that there would be a list of all those people who had been captured in the industrial zone of Karakaj. And at the school in Karakaj, at the Alhos factory, these different places were used as camps. And then I went back, and then together with my associates I made a list of about 250 names. We passed this list on by messenger, and there was a brief cease-fire while he took that. And after that, I got a letter from Branko Grujic and Major Marko Pavlovic. He was -- Marko Pavlovic, the commander of the defence of Zvornik. His real name was actually Branko Popovic. He was an officer of the JNA from Novi Sad. Actually, he was in charge of the defence of Zvornik. And literally they had written that they have no information about captured Muslims in these camps and that they cannot carry out this transaction. Again, there was another letter that I wrote in which I asked them firmly to furnish this information. They replied that they were unable to do that. And then after that, I made a priority list based on this other list, a priority list of 40 people of whom we knew were in the camps. Somebody had seen them, somebody who had escaped, that they were in the camp. So I sent this list of 40 people, and they said that they agreed, they would send those people for exchange, but we would then have to give some people back. The process of exchange was organised. Serbian soldiers were properly placed in body-bags and brought to the line of separation in simple transport -- by simple transport means, and then when the exchange was supposed to take place, there was actually a trick, and an attack took place from that other side. There were three and a half thousand civilians there. The exchange failed. In the second attempt, the exchange was successful. The truck arrived, and then people started to come out from under the tarpaulin from the truck, and then we counted 12 people with plastic bags on their heads.
